Boniface VIII. Born Benedetto Caetani, he reigned as pope from 1294 to 1303. He is remembered for his extreme claims of papal supremacy and his disastrous conflicts with the rising nation-states of Europe, particularly France. His papacy marks the beginning of the decline of medieval papal political hegemony.

In 1302, he issued the papal bull Unam Sanctam, which asserted absolute papal supremacy, declaring that both spiritual and temporal powers are under the Pope's authority and that submission to the Pope is necessary for salvation. He also initiated the first Jubilee or Holy Year in 1300, offering a plenary indulgence to thousands of Christian pilgrims who visited Rome.

Boniface engaged in a bitter taxation conflict with King Philip IV of France, issuing the bull Clericis Laicos in 1296 to forbid secular rulers from taxing the clergy without papal permission. In 1303, he was captured and assaulted at his palace in Anagni by French soldiers led by Guillaume de Nogaret and the Colonna family in what became known as the Outrage of Anagni. He died in Rome weeks later. Even before his death, Dante placed him in the eighth circle of Hell among the simoniacs in his Inferno, depicting him as a buyer and seller of church offices. His arrest by French forces at Anagni shortly before his death paved the way for the Avignon Papacy.
